title: The Canarese War
html:
THE CANARESE WAR*

BY

T. PONNAMBALAM PILLAI ESQ., M.R.A.S.

IN spite of the fact that the Dravidians were the possessors of a civilization even more ancient than that of the Aryans, the history of that part of India occupied by them is still enshrouded in mystery. It is to be regretted that even the times within the memory of man are in that cimmerian darkness. Any attempt to remove this veil should be welcome.

While I had been making researches in the history of this ancient land, I came across a cultured young gentleman—a scion of an ancient family in South Travancore which gave a Prime Minister to that estate—who had been silently working towards the same end. He placed at my disposal a few manuscripts of popular songs, which certain classes of people in that part of the country sing in the months of November and December, to the accompaniment of a lyre in the form of a bow, which has consequently given the poems the name of Vil Adichan Pattu meaning songs of the beater of bow, and requested me to make out what I could with the aid of the scanty knowledge of Tamil I possessed.

The heading of the most important of the manuscripts is 'Cannadian Pêr' (കണ്ഠമുധന്ത പോറി) which means the War of the Canarese. The verses are evidently in heroic metre and I do not think they are to be found committed to writing. The copies before me were taken down as they were recited. through the efforts of my young friend, in the form they were handed down from mouth to mouth by the unlettered. They, therefore, defy all rules of grammar and prosody, though there are sure signs of their having conformed to them once. The poem gives an account of an unreturned royal love, and the consequent invasion of the dominions of the offending monarch. The actual scene of operations was between South Travancore, and a line drawn in the Tinnevelly District from Tuticorin to Shermadevi, and from there to the hills which form part of the Western Ghauts.

The difficulty that would confront one in a matter like this is the assigning of dates to the events narrated in the folk songs. From the fact that the expedition was despatched by the Canarese king of Mysore, it is but natural to conclude that he must have belonged to the Nava-Bellala dynasty which became extinct towards the close of the fourteenth century of the Christian era. Again from the fact that an embassy was despatched to the Chera king at Tiruvanjikalam, one may be tempted to carry the events to a time before the tenth century. But as the Vijayanagar kings were of Vaduga and Cannada descent, it is likely that the king referred to was of that line, and the generals referred to were some of his own or of the Naick Viceroys of Madura. I believe, the latter is the view of Professor Rengaswamy Iyengar of the Maharajah's College, Trivandram, and it is what I infer from an article of Mr. V. Rangachariar that appeared in the Wednesday Review of the 2nd February, 1910. In case the events are assigned to the Naick period, they must have transpired during the time of Viswanath Naick, the founder of the dynasty. For, it was he that fought with the last of the Pandyas; the chief participators in the military operations as recorded in the manuscripts were the Canarese Generals, on one side, and the members of the Pandyan family stationed at Va||iyūr, in the Nanguneri Taluq of the Tinnevelly District and eleven miles from the borders of Travancore, on the other. I shall not say further on the subject and leave it to others more competent.

Now to the story as given in the manuscripts. The ministers of Kulasêkhara Pândyan, fearing an attack from the Canarese Generals, advised their king to retire to his southern capital Va||iyûr, and so he did. About this time some minstrels going about from house to house to earn their livelihood by singing popular songs and exhibiting representations of men and places, one day obtained admittance into the Canarese court, and depicted in high-flown metres the personal accomplishments of the Pandyan, and made an effective scenic representation of his likeness before the maiden daughter of the king. She at once became infatuated with love, repaired to the august presence of her father, and spoke in unequivocal terms that either she should make the young Kulasêkhara as her wedded lord or become herself a prey to fire. The king was alarmed at the attitude of his daughter; and without losing time, he despatched an envoy offering Kulasêkhara her hand along with the kingdom that extended from 'Benares to Cape Comorin' and 'all the paraphernalia belonging to that exalted position'. The envoy started at once on his eventful mission and, after traversing various parts of the ancient Chola and Pandyan kingdoms, reached Valliyur where he was ushered into the royal presence at the appointed time, and in due form. When he was interrogated as to the object of his mission, he stated it. The Pandyan scoffed at the idea of making an alliance with a family that was of plebian origin, and with which his ancestors had not formed any connection. The envoy pressed the request of his employer; but the prince was inexorable, and told him to go about his business. He, however, took care to observe the etiquette of his court and to command his ministers to make him the usual presents before dismissing him. Disappointed and crest-fallen as he was, the Canarese envoy left the Pandyan court and reached Dwarasamudram in eighteen days and related all that had taken place. While doing so, he gave a graphic account of the Pandyan country, his great cities including his capital, his fort, his court and his personal accomplishments. The daughter of the king as she listend to it with wrapt attention, became still more infatuated, and pined away so as to lose her health. Intimation was given to her father as to the state of her health. He sent for his daughter and, assuring her that he would endeavour to secure Kulasekhara for her husband, despatched the same envoy on a second mission to secure the object in view. Kulasekhara reaffirmed his previous reply, and peremptorily ordered the royal messenger to clear out of his presence. On this the Pandyan Prime Minister proposed to put him to disgrace, but the prince declined to be a party to such an unkindly act. The Minister, however, took occasion to read a sermon to the envoy to impress upon him the antiquity of the royal line unlike that of his employer and the great prowess of the Pandyan dynasty in the art of war, not to say of its skill in the arts of peace. The ambassador again returned to Mysore disappointed, and related to his king all that had taken place. The result was a declaration of war.

The King collected a large army composed of different nationalities from all parts of the empire from 'Benares to Cape Comorin' and set out with it on an auspicious day, after propitiating the deities for the success of his arms. His daughter was an important factor in the camp and she was there ready to wed the accomplished Kulasekhara, as soon as he fell into the trap laid by her father. The results of the war were not attained in a day, for it was a protracted struggle. It may be divided into three compaigns:—

First: Up to the fall of Vailliyür Fort.

Second: The rule of Othachy (Othachy), brother of the Canarese king as Viceroy, over Valliyür and the desultory warfare that took place for a long period. It closed with his death, and the retaking of the fort of Vaĥliyūr by the Pandyan armies.

Third: The defeat of the last of the Pandyans and extermination of that dynasty.

I shall deal with each campaign one by one. The first was not of short duration. It extended for about a year. The march of the Mysore army through the Chōla dominions was smooth-sailing as there were no opposing forces. In the Pandyan kingdom too, some semblance of authority was maintained only towards the extreme south. Till the army reached Poĥtaputhūr (which in reality is Vaĥtaputhūr w̄d̄d̄p̄l̄ḡāi) there were no encounters. The Pandyan army was concentrated in that place, and the various divisions of it were placed under the command of four brothers and a nephew of Kulasēkhara. In the battle that ensued, the Canarese force was defeated, and it took refuge at Vaĥukachymalai (w̄d̄s̄k̄s̄m̄w̄). As it was nearer to Vaĥliyūr the Pandyan army marched on to that place, to concentrate all its strength, and make a determined stand. Operations were commenced early on the following morning, and the respective forces were led by the nephews of the two kings. After a well-contested battle in which a large number of Mysoreans were left dead on the field, the Canarese were completely routed, and they again took refuge at Vaĥukachymalai. Finding the disconcerted state in which his daughter was, the Canarese king assured her that he would leave no stone unturned to compass her object.

The next thing he did was to propitiate the evil spirits. While he was engaged in that pursuit with his immense force, spies informed Kulasēkhara that the attention of his enemy was diverted. He ordered his generals to attack him and they accordingly did so. The battle was again hotly contested. When arrays of Canarese men were discomfited, they were readily and persistently replaced by others. The victory was however with the Pandyan army.

There was a pause. The Canarese generals were refitting their army by collecting all the stragglers and deserters together, and by replacing those slaughtered in the field, by means of levies from Mysore. But their king was again engaged in propitiating the evil spirits, and using the 'black art' to secure victory. On consulting a traitorous astrologer who seceded from the Pandyan camp, he declared in favour of the Mysoreans. While these events were transpiring in the camp of the Canarese king, the Pandyan was seeking a place of refuge in case of reverse. The chief minister Kālingavillan advocated the occupation of the fort at Chorimuttan-pārai (சேரிலுத்தன்பான்ற) in the possession of Chêra. It is one that was once built by the Pandyân, and had a zig-zig approach in which lay its safety. It appears to have gone into the hands of Chêra, as a result of conquest. His sanction was therefore necessary to occupy it.

Though the Pandyan hesitated to go into the fort at the Chorimuttan-pārai, he did send his women and treasure. This place is in the Zemindary of Chingampatty, not far away from the sacred falls of Banathirtham. The manuscripts referred to communications with Neḍumangād, which is twelve miles from Trevandrum on one side and the Malayankulam (மழையான்குளம்) plains on the other. In Travancore, Neḍumangād is the nearest inhabited point that can be reached from Chorimuttan-pārai, through the Ponmudi Hills and Kallar. Malayankulam is about seven miles from Ambasamudram at the foot of the ghauts on the eastern side and it came into possession of the Travancore sovereigns probably as the successors of the last of the Pandyans. Till 1831 it was with that kingdom, but was ceded about that time to the British Government. All that is now left of the sovereignty of it are two ruined temples, the presiding dieties of which are receiving starvation allowance.

Kulasêkhara was now free to fight, having got rid of all encumbrances. The Mysoreans were also ready after a lapse of six months to resume hostilities. Early on a morning the Canarese force laid siege to the fort of Vaḷḷiyūr. The Pandyan army defended it with all the might in its power. The brothers of the king and his nephew with the leading generals were posted at each of the fort gates. The battle raged fiercely. The armies were composed of infantry, cavalry, and elephant trains. The weapons that were used were bows and arrows, swords and lances. At the heat of the battle, the Pandyan thought that it was not fair to have the fort gates closed, and he accordingly caused them to be opened. The Canarese entered the fort. When the two opposing forces closed together there was hand to hand fight. In the hotly contested combat, the nephew (sister's son) of the Pandyan was slain. Though this event paralysed the action for a time, it emboldened him to try further conclusions. He therefore took the command himself, and led 40,000 horses, into the heart of the opposing army which spread itself between Vaḷḷiyūr and Vaḍukachymalai. This was one of the most sanguinary engagements, as it was one of vengeance. Kulasēkhara himself slew a large number of his enemies—men and horses, and the son of the Canarese king himself fell a victim to his sword. And the Cararese army was panic-stricken and fled, leaving the killed and wounded there. It seems that the soldiers of the defeated army were driven out as far as Veeravanallūr and the king and his staff encamped themselves with the remnant of his men on the plains of Callūr.

It must be noted here that throughout the struggle, though the Pandyan army was victorious, the false steps taken by the king and his ministers had all the effects of a defeat. Even after this battle Kulasēkhara was advised to quit Vaḷḷiyūr and seek the stronghold where he had sent his women and treasure. He was personally averse to taking such a step, but the force of circumstances compelled him to accept the proferred advice. The Canarese army followed on his heels and a battle ensued in which the Pandyan king lost another great general in the person of his brother—Tikkelām Pugalum Perumāl (திக்கேலாம் பக்கும் பெருமான்). There was a lull. The Canarese army was encamped on the plains of Malayankulam and the Pandyan continued to remain in his aery at Chorimuttan-pārai. Both were unwilling to attack each other. The Canarese king tried to inveigle the Pandyan to descend to the plains from his fastness, and give one more battle, but his attempt was doomed to failure. After remaining inactive at the place for months he made up his mind to repair to Valīyiūr, and set his brother on the throne of Kulasēkhara. Accordingly he went to the place, put his brother in charge of Valīyiūr and returned to Mysore.

Second Campaign :—Kulasēkhara Pandyan spent some years at Chorimuttan-pārai, and afterwards established himself at Thōvālai, in South Travancore, constructing a fort there, and extended his rule as far as Kōttār. Thus some years passed. The Canarese Viceroy at Valliyūr, Othachy, had not forgotten the aim of his brother, whose daughter yet remained a virgin, expecting to obtain the hand of Kulasēkhara. Information reached him of the movement of Kulasēkhara. He collected a large army and encamped at Muppandal close to the present frontiers of Travancore. On hearing this, the Pandyan prepared himself to meet him, and at the same time detatched a force to Kōttār that it may not be taken by a coup de main. The Mysoreans gradually approached the fort of Thōvālai and besieged it. A cannonade was opened and at last a breach was made in the wall. The Canarese men entered the fort and a fierce encounter took place. The Pandyan men wavered. While the zeal was flagging, timely assistance was afforded by the archers of Quilon and the lancers composed of the Ambalapulai Panikers. The situation was changed. The Mysoreans now faltered. They were routed and driven as far as Ilanguḷam (இளக்குளம்) and their leader was left dead in the field. After this victory Kulasēkhara re-entered the fort of Valīyiūr and took charge of his lost kingdom.

Third Campaign:—Due intimation was conveyed to the Canarese king at Mysore of what had transpired. It was too much for him to bear. He at once started with a large army vowing vengeance, traversed the Chola and Pandyan countries as fast as he could, reached Mankaikād (மந்பைக்கொடு), united his forces with those of his late brother and engaged the Pandyan army on the plains of Mānāmguḷam (மாலுத்குளம்) and fought valiantly. Kulasēkhara and his brother knew that they were fighting for their life, and they behaved therefore in the battlefield with admirable courage. The carnage was terrible. Pachai-Perumal and Peria-Odayar, two of the brothers of Kulasēkhara, sacrificed their lives heroically. This proved an incentive to the Pandyan and his surviving brothers to fight more valiantly. They went on hacking to pieces the enemy's men. The bloodshed was terrible. But the opposing forces were overwhelming. The Pandyan applied to Chèra for assistance, but for some unaccountable reason it was not granted. At last he was compelled to retreat to Vaḷliyūr towards evening. Very early on the following morning he left it for his fastness with his immediate followers, and his valuables, leaving his remaining brothers and generals to continue the fight; at dawn on the following day hostilities were resumed, and they were carried on with the same vigour as on the previous day. The brothers and the leading generals except Kālingavillan (காவித்கவில்லன்) fell fighting desperately.

On receiving intimation of the long expected catastrophe, Kulasēkhara thought that it was but right that he should proceed to the battlefield and take up the command of the army; but he felt that he was not destined to return. He therefore summoned all his seven wives to the side of the tank where he used to perform his ablutions, mentioned to them the errand on which he was going and requested them to remain in the fort with peace of mind till his return. But they knew what was to happen to their lord and king, and told him that they would rather lay their hand on their own lives, than be in a state of suspense. The king then assured them of meeting them in a week's time in a different sphere, and assented to the course proposed to be adopted by them. At this, the ladies entered the tank and drowned themselves. When the king was sure that life was extinct he caused the bodies to be placed on funeral pyres. After they were reduced to ashes, and performing the necessary rites, he found that he greatly relieved in mind and proceeded to the battle-field. There he found his faithful minister and commander-in-chief, Kälingavillan, awaiting his arrival. He requested the Pandyan for permission to take the command and it was granted. He fought most bravely for hours and brought down with his hand many heroes, and he himself succumbed at last. It was then the turn of Kulasêkhara, and he performed his duty with alacrity, and fought with the courage characteristic of his race. The Canarese king knew what the Pandyan was about, and warned his men against doing any harm in any way to his person. To enable them to approach him and sieze him without harming him, and themselves, he enjoined them to wearmail-coats. After a sanguinary encounter they surrounded him, made a captive of him put him in a palanquin, closed it carefully and took the valuable prize to their-master. In the flush of success it did not occur to the Canarese warriors, to disarm their prisoner. For he had a pocket knife, and with it he cut his throat on the way, and put an end to his life. As soon as the Pandyan was made a prisoner, that news was conveyed to the camp of the Canarese king, where he and his daughter were rejoicing over the event and loaded with presents those who took the glad tidings. The precious treasure in the palanquin was being momentarily expected, and when it reached the royal presence what was found was only the mortal remains of the last of the Pandyans. The princess viewed it with composure and realized that the account given to her by the ministrels of the personal accomplishments of Kulasêkhara was in no way exaggerated. She reconciled herself to her fate, and requested her father to cremate the body and allow her to ascend the funeral pyre, as if she were the wedded wife of the Pandyan. It was granted and another tragedy was brought to a close.

The account which has just been concluded is no fable. Though the manuscripts are full of exaggerations and supernaturalisms, I have sifted what I considered to be historical facts. The three South Indian dynasties were connected with one another from time immemorial by marriage, and about the eleventh century A. D. the Chola and the Pandyan became merged into one another. At the present moment no traces of them are to be found anywhere, for both the races have become extinct. Owing to conquest and other causes the original stock was corrupted and the hybrids of the main lines ceased to exist early, while the collaterals lingered here and there with a show of some vitality. These also collapsed as in the case of the Pandyan family at Vaĥliyūr.
